findings.claim: Pope Pius XI declared in 1930 that “every sexual act must be within a framework of marriage.”
findings.truth: Pius XI's 1930 encyclical is Casti Connubii, but it contains no such sentence. Its actual wording (para 18) is that “every use of the faculty given by God for the procreation of new life is the right and the privilege of the married state alone... and must be confined absolutely within the sacred limits of that state”. The lesson presents a paraphrase inside quotation marks as a papal quotation.
findings.evidence: vatican.va full text of Casti Connubii (Pius XI, 31 December 1930), searched for the quoted sentence

findings.claim: Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2013.
findings.truth: The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 received Royal Assent on 17 July 2013, but the marriage provisions came into force on 13 March 2014 and the first same-sex weddings took place on 29 March 2014. Couples could not marry in 2013.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 - commencement table

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: “The seventh: 'You shall not commit adultery' (Exodus 20:14).”
findings.truth: “You shall not commit adultery” is the seventh commandment in the Jewish and most Protestant numberings, but the sixth in the Catholic and Lutheran numberings. The lesson teaches Catholic positions throughout, so a bare “the seventh” is a wrong attribution for Catholic students.
findings.evidence: standard Catholic numbering (Catechism, Sixth Commandment covers adultery and chastity)

findings.claim: The Qur’an itself acknowledges this is difficult: “You will never be able to be equal between wives, even if it is your ardent desire” (4:129).
findings.truth: The reference is right but the quotation matches no published translation. It welds the first half of Sahih International (“never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives”) onto the second half of Yusuf Ali (“even if it is your ardent desire”). The Clear Quran reads “You will never be able to maintain justice between your wives - no matter how keen you are.” Safest fix is to drop the quotation marks and keep the reference.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: “1994 (with female bishops permitted from 2015).”
findings.truth: Women bishops were permitted in the Church of England from 2014, when the enabling Measure was approved and came into force. 2015 is the year the first woman bishop was consecrated, not the year they were permitted. The body text of the lesson (“female bishops since 2015”) is right; only the flashcard is wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Ordination of women in the Anglican Communion - Church of England row: consecration of female bishops permitted 2014, first female bishop 2015

findings.claim: The British Humanist Association actively campaigns for LGBTQ+ rights.
findings.truth: The British Humanist Association changed its operating name to Humanists UK in May 2017. A student naming the BHA today is naming a body that no longer uses that name.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Humanists UK - “In May 2017, the BHA changed its operating name to Humanists UK”

findings.claim: Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2013.
findings.truth: Same as F2. The Act is dated 2013; same-sex couples could not actually marry until 13 March 2014, with the first weddings on 29 March 2014.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 - commencement table

findings.claim: The three contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships required by AQA are: (1) conservative Christians oppose them... (2) liberal Christians accept them... and (3) Islam opposes them...
findings.truth: The spec sets THREE ISSUES (contraception, sexual relationships before marriage, same-sex relationships), not three beliefs on one issue. On each issue students must explain contrasting beliefs “with reference to the main religious tradition in Britain (Christianity) and one or more other religious traditions”, and the exam question asks for TWO contrasting beliefs. As written, the key fact invites a student to answer with conservative plus liberal Christian views only, which are both from the same tradition and would not meet the requirement.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.1 Theme A (lines 1187-1196) and 4.4.2 Component 2 (one five-part question of 1, 1, 4, 6, 12 marks)

findings.claim: Always include a specific scripture reference to push into the top marks. (advice given for the 4-mark contrasting-beliefs question)
findings.truth: The 4-mark question awards up to 2 marks per belief for a statement plus development. It carries no requirement to cite a source. Requiring sacred writings is the 6-mark question (“Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching”). The claim invents a mark-scheme rule and sends students hunting for quotations that earn nothing.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 and 3.2.1 - the source-of-authority requirement sits on the 6-mark question only

findings.claim: In Britain, divorce is common - roughly 42% of marriages end in divorce.
findings.truth: 42% is the older ONS projection for marriages formed around 2012 and is still widely printed in GCSE textbooks. More recent ONS cohort projections are lower. Not wrong enough to change without a verified replacement figure, but it is a stale statistic.
findings.evidence: no replacement figure verified this session (WebSearch budget exhausted)

findings.claim: zinah: “Unlawful sexual activity in Islam, including adultery, sex before marriage and homosexual acts.” (repeated in L3 content and glossary)
findings.truth: Classical Islamic jurisprudence generally treats liwat (same-sex acts) separately from zina, and the schools differ on whether the zina penalty applies. GCSE textbooks commonly use the wider definition the lesson gives. Options: leave the textbook simplification, or narrow the definition to sexual activity outside marriage and describe same-sex acts as haram separately.
findings.evidence: classification disputed between the fiqh schools; no single settled position to correct to
findings.ruling: Leave: unsourced replacement / textbook usage / quotation provenance (source queue).

findings.claim: Abdul Wahid Hamid: “The only way to protect all within society is to maintain a society where only a man and his wife share the act of sex.” (L1) and the Methodist Church: “responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.” (L3)
findings.truth: Both are standard GCSE textbook quotations but neither could be traced to a primary source this session. Options: keep them as they are, or keep the substance and drop the quotation marks so nothing is attributed verbatim to a named source we cannot cite.
findings.evidence: no primary source located; WebSearch budget exhausted
findings.ruling: Leave: unsourced replacement / textbook usage / quotation provenance (source queue).

findings.claim: Common reasons include adultery, unreasonable behaviour, growing apart, financial problems and domestic abuse.
findings.truth: Correct as reasons why marriages break down, so no edit. Worth knowing that “adultery” and “unreasonable behaviour” were the pre-2022 legal grounds; England and Wales moved to no-fault divorce on 6 April 2022, and the unit teaches no UK divorce law at all.
findings.evidence: Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020, in force 6 April 2022

summary: All three lessons carry findings: two HIGH (a papal quotation that Casti Connubii does not contain, and a Qur'an 4:129 quotation welded from two translations), five MEDIUM (same-sex marriage dated 2013 in two lessons, the commandment numbering, the women-bishops date, the retired British Humanist Association name, plus two exam-framing errors in Lesson 3). Scripture references, knowledge-check keys and the 1/1/4/6/12 practice structure are otherwise sound.
